3798:
The Bible twice quotes a Book of Jasher (Hebrew Yashar, upright). Joshua 10:13 cites it for the poetic command, Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and Moon, in the Valley of Aijalon. Second Samuel 1:18 says David's lament over Saul and Jonathan (How the mighty have fallen) was written in it. The Greek text of 1 Kings 8:53 also cites a Book of the Song for Solomon's dedication words, and many scholars think this is the same book with two Hebrew letters swapped (shir, song, for yashar). It appears to have been an anthology of national poetry honouring Israel's heroes.

The original is lost. Several later books have borrowed the name and should not be confused with it: a Hebrew midrash Sefer ha-Yashar printed in Venice in 1625 (a medieval retelling of Genesis to Judges, translated into English in 1840 and reprinted by Latter-day Saints and others), and an English forgery of 1751 by Jacob Ilive claiming to be translated by Alcuin. Neither is the ancient book.

The books sold today as the Book of Jasher are later works, one a medieval Jewish retelling and one an 18th-century forgery. The original is gone.

The books of Kings repeatedly end a king's reign with a formula: the rest of his acts, and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles (literally the matters of the days) of the Kings of Israel, or of Judah? The first is cited about 18 times, the second about 15, and a Book of the Acts of Solomon once. The phrase is first used of Jeroboam I (1 Kgs 14:19).

These were evidently fuller records, perhaps official annals or a popular history based on them, that readers could consult for wars, building projects and conspiracies. The biblical author chose from them what served his theological purpose: whether each king did right or evil in the eyes of the LORD. They are not the same as our canonical books of 1-2 Chronicles, which were written later and cite their own sources.

First Chronicles 29:29 says the acts of King David from first to last are written in the records (literally the words) of Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet and Gad the seer. Second Chronicles cites more prophetic works in the same way: Nathan, the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite and the visions of Iddo the seer for Solomon (9:29), the records of Shemaiah and Iddo for Rehoboam (12:15), the words of Jehu son of Hanani (20:34), what Isaiah wrote of Uzziah (26:22) and the words of the seers for Manasseh's prayer (33:19).

Scholars debate whether these were separate prophetic books or sections of a larger history of the kings, labelled by the prophet active in each reign (the Chronicler sometimes says one prophet's words were taken up into the Book of the Kings, 2 Chr 20:34). Either way, Chronicles assumes that prophets were Israel's historians, which later Jewish tradition reflected in calling Joshua to Kings the Former Prophets and in the Talmud's claim that Samuel, Nathan and Gad completed the books of Samuel.

3923:
Paul's own letters mention letters we do not have. In 1 Corinthians 5:9 he refers to an earlier letter telling the Corinthians not to associate with sexually immoral people, which they had misunderstood. In 2 Corinthians 2:3-4 and 7:8 he recalls a letter written with many tears that grieved them; some scholars identify it with 1 Corinthians, others with a lost letter, and others with 2 Corinthians 10-13. Colossians 4:16 tells the Colossians to read the letter from Laodicea. Paul also warns against letters forged in his name (2 Thess 2:2).

The letter from Laodicea has attracted much discussion. Some think it is our Ephesians, a circular letter (several early manuscripts lack in Ephesus in Eph 1:1, and Marcion called Ephesians the letter to the Laodiceans). Others think it is lost, or less likely Philemon. A short Latin Epistle to the Laodiceans, stitched together from phrases in Philippians and Galatians, circulated widely in medieval Latin Bibles and even early printed German Bibles, but it is universally regarded as a later forgery. The Muratorian Fragment already warned of a letter to the Laodiceans forged for Marcion's sect.

Some may be hidden inside letters we have, like Ephesians, but others are simply lost. A later fake Letter to the Laodiceans circulated in the Middle Ages but is not by Paul.

3965: The Didache is a short church handbook from around the time the last New Testament books were written. It teaches a simple way of life, then explains how to baptise, fast, pray the Lord's Prayer, share the Lord's Supper and test travelling preachers. It was never Scripture, but it shows what ordinary Christian congregations actually did very early on.
3966:
The Didache (Greek for "teaching") is the oldest surviving Christian church manual. It opens with the "Two Ways" - a way of life and a way of death - a moral teaching built on the double love command and the Sermon on the Mount, with lists of sins to avoid. It then gives practical instructions: baptise in running water if possible, in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit; fast on Wednesdays and Fridays rather than the days other groups used; pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day; give thanks over the cup and bread with short prayers that never mention Jesus' death directly. It ends with rules for welcoming apostles and prophets (a true prophet who asks for money or stays more than two days is a false one), appointing bishops and deacons, and a short warning about the end of the age.

The Didache was known by name in the early church but was lost to modern readers until 1873, when Philotheos Bryennios found a complete copy in an eleventh-century manuscript (dated 1056) in Constantinople; he published it in 1883. Since then it has become one of the most discussed early Christian texts, because it seems to come from a community that knew Matthew-like Jesus tradition, still lived close to Jewish practice, and organised itself without a single dominant bishop.

3968: The way of death: a list of vices (ch. 5)

3975: The Didache does not claim to be written by any apostle; its title only says it passes on the apostles' teaching, and scholars agree it was compiled by unnamed teachers. It was also never used widely enough as Scripture. Eusebius (*Church History* 3.25) put "the so-called Teachings of the Apostles" among the "spurious" or disputed books - orthodox and useful, but not genuine apostolic Scripture. Athanasius in 367 left it out of his canon list and placed it among books "to be read" by new converts. That middle category, rather than outright rejection, is the best description of its status in every tradition. (Here "read-not-canon" means respected and edifying, not Scripture; in the Ethiopian church Didache material survives inside later church orders rather than as a separate book.)

Its Two Ways teaching influenced later church orders (the *Apostolic Constitutions* of the fourth century reworked it), and its teaching against abortion and infanticide (Didache 2.2) is one of the earliest Christian statements on the subject. Historians value it as a window on a Jewish-Christian community still forming its practices.
